study.title: Leviticus 6 - Restitution, Continuous Fire and Holiness of Deliverance
study.overview: Leviticus 6 gathers instructions on three central areas of the cult and life of the people: the reparation of damage committed against others, priestly care with burnt offerings and cereals, and the rules of sin atonement. The chapter shows that the holiness of God reaches both daily ethics and worship. Sin against the like is not treated as a merely social matter, because it also offends the Lord. At the same time, worship requires order, continuity and distinction between what can be eaten and what must be totally burned. The emphasis lies on concrete reparation, priestly mediation and reverence in the face of divine holiness.

outline.title: Refund for guilt against the next
outline.explanation: The first verses deal with sins such as fraud, theft, extortion, deposit retention, appropriation of the find and false oath. The culprit must return what he took, add a fifth, and then bring a ram without ram for atonement. The text unites horizontal reparation and forgiveness before God.

outline.title: Law of burnt-offering, cereals and continuous fire
outline.explanation: Here the instruction is addressed to the priests. The burnt offering must remain in continuous fire on the altar, with reverent cleansing of the ashes. The grain offering is partly burned and the rest belongs to the priests, but it must be eaten in a holy place and without leaven. The text highlights order, separation and provision for ministers.

outline.title: Offer of cereals in priestly ordering
outline.explanation: The offering of Aaron and his sons on the day of anointing is presented as a perpetual portion, divided between morning and afternoon. But in the case of the anointed priest, all the offering is burned and not eaten. The difference highlights the priest's special dedication and the exclusive nature of the rite.

outline.title: Law of atonement for sin and prohibition of eating certain offerings
outline.explanation: The last section regulates the sin offering: place of slaughter, who can eat, the sanctifying effect of contact with the flesh, and the care of blood and utensils. But some offerings for sin, especially those whose blood is taken to the tabernacle to reconcile in the sanctuary, should not be eaten; they must be burned. The distinction preserves the sanctity of the most solemn atonement.

study.context: The chapter presupposes the sacrificial system of Israel under the mediation of Moses and Aaron, with the tabernacle as the center of worship. The notes provided indicate that the instructions begin with cases of damage and false oath among ordinary people and then begin to guide priests on specific procedures. It is also mentioned that the fire of the altar should remain lit continuously, and that some sacrifices had different rules according to the species and the function of the offerer.
study.theology: Leviticus 6 teaches that sin is never only private: injustice against others is at the same time offense against the Lord. Therefore, biblical repentance includes real reparation, not just verbal confession. Restitution with an increase of a fifth shows that God's righteousness is not content with remorse, but requires restoration of harm. The chapter also emphasizes the holiness of worship: the continuous fire, the proper use of the garments, the holy place to eat certain offerings, and the total burning of others reveal that the approach of God is not casual. The atonement, although offering forgiveness, does not trivialize divine holiness; on the contrary, it structures access to forgiveness through mediation and obedience. The distinction between offerings that can be eaten and offerings that must be fully burned shows that reconciliation with God has different forms according to the gravity and purpose of sacrifice.

scholarViews.insight: The text shows that there is no "secular" sin: the harm against another person also involves offense to God, and reparation to the harmed must come before the pursuit of forgiveness.
The instructions pass from the offerings to the priests, showing that even those who serve in worship are under commandment and must obey the rules laid down by God.
The rule on the addition of a fifth when the refund is made voluntarily highlights that the law provides for calculated and careful redress in cases of fraud or undue retention.

questions: In what situations can I be dealing with as a single human matter what God also considers an offense against him?
Does my repentance practice include concrete restitution when I caused harm to someone?
What does the order of continuous fire and the rules of holiness on the altar teach me about constancy and reverence in worship?
study.practice: Examine your life in the light of this chapter in three steps: confess sins that involve injustice against anyone; do your best to repair harm with honesty, generosity and speed; and cultivate a life of reverent and constant worship, remembering that God's holiness reaches both his words and his actions. If there is something to return, don't delay. If there is something to be corrected in worship or devotion, organize to obey more faithfully.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are partial in some verses and do not detail all the symbols of the offerings. There is also a limit recognized in the notes on the textual division of the chapter between numbering traditions, especially the observation that some scholars understand that the chapter begins at 6:8 in the original arrangement. It is not possible to affirm, based only on the notes, symbolic meanings more specific than those explicitly mentioned.
